newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian military riven by political tensions.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian military riven by political tensions.

text.p: Top Cambodian army officers continued trading verbal attacks on Thursday, raising concerns the military has become dangerously divided between feuding co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen.
In the past three days, military brass have held duelling press conferences, accused each other of assassination plots and alleged illegal logging activities.
"This is the beginning of real divisions in the military," said parliamentarian Ahmad Yahya.
"I think this will go on until the elections," he added, referring to national elections scheduled for 1998 that will likely pit the co-premiers against each other.
The military's public disputes erupted on Monday after Ranariddh was forced to cancel a trip to Samlaut, a base of former Khmer Rouge in Cambodia's northwest, over security concerns.

Most of the Khmer Rouge defectors there have pledged support to Hun Sen, and senior military officers said a local commander had threatened fighting and that villagers were blocked from greeting Ranariddh.

On Wednesday deputy chief of staff Lieutenant General Nhiek Bun Chhay held a news conference and accused General Keo Pong, a former Khmer Rouge commander who has been Hun Sen's point man for recruiting the Samlaut defectors, of creating the security problem to hide illegal logging activities.
On Thursday, Keo Pong held his own news conference and accused a general loyal to Ranariddh of trying to assassinate him.
Keo Pong claimed General Serey Kosal, deputy governor of the northwest province of Battambang, on Wednesday ordered him shot at the provincial airport.

"Yesterday there were around 40 solders surrounding me at Battambang airport, putting their fingers on their gun triggers, and Serey Kosal shouted at the co-Ministers of Defence (Tea Banh and Tea Chamrath), '(I) want to shoot Keo Pong'," Keo Pong said.
But Serey Kosal said: "I only pointed at him and called him a worthless man. But I didn't want to shoot him out of anger, I just wanted to search for his authorisation papers."

Analysts said the controversy reveals that tensions between the co-premiers have spread into the military, generating increasing scepticism about the future of the fragile coalition formed following U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.
Ranariddh and Hun Sen have clashed over a variety of issues, from power sharing to competition to recruit Khmer Rouge defectors to their sides.
The Khmer Rouge, which led the brutal 1975-1979 "killing fields" regime, have been decimated by waves of defections in recent months. Only about 800 to 2,000 hardline rebels remain.
The Khmer Rouge had signed a 1991 peace pact with the government, but later reneged on the deal and have been fighting the coalition government since 1993.
